title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
An AI-powered issue triage system deployed in Cline's development workflow accepted and executed commands injected through GitHub issue titles without validating the input. The system allowed anyone with a GitHub account to craft malicious issues that the AI would interpret as legitimate instructions, leading to execution of arbitrary code in the CI/CD pipeline. This failure happened at the boundary between user input and automated command execution, where a human review step before the AI acted on external input would have caught the injection.

The vulnerability persisted for over two months because security reports sent to Cline starting January 1, 2026, went unanswered. The system was used outside the conditions it should have been deployed under: an AI making decisions about code execution from untrusted sources without human verification. Once disclosed publicly, the vulnerability was patched within an hour, but the delay left a window where the attacker surface was exposed to anyone who knew it existed.

It is not established that unauthorized code was successfully published to package repositories, though credential theft is suspected.

summary:
# Summary

Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, contained a critical security vulnerability from December 21, 2025, to February 9, 2026. Researchers discovered that the company's AI-powered issue triage system allowed anyone with a GitHub account to inject malicious commands into issue titles, tricking the AI into executing arbitrary code. This code could then poison the GitHub Actions cache to steal publication credentials and push malware to the VS Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM repositories, potentially compromising millions of developer installations.

The researcher attempted to contact Cline's security team multiple times starting January 1, 2026, without receiving a response. After public disclosure on February 9, 2026, Cline fixed the vulnerability within one hour and rotated all publishing credentials. Evidence suggests an actor may have successfully exploited the vulnerability and obtained valid credentials, though no malicious updates were published. Cline has since advised users to disable automatic updates until the company confirms no unauthorized access occurred.
